section.title: Woe to the City of Blood
section.sectionRationale: The book's final oracle, a sustained woe over Nineveh. Nahum indicts the city of blood, exposes her as a seductive harlot, points to fallen Thebes as her mirror, and mocks her merchants and officials as locusts that vanish. It ends not with hope for Nineveh but with the applause of all who had suffered her endless cruelty.
section.thesis: Nineveh, the bloody city of lies and seduction, will fall as surely as Thebes did; there is no healing for her wound, and all who hear of it will clap, for none escaped her constant cruelty.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the woe over the city of blood; God exposing the harlot; the warning from fallen Thebes; the locust hordes that flee; and the final dirge over an incurable wound.

units.label: Woe to the city of blood
units.note: the whip, the wheel, the heaps of slain

verses.text: {{hoy|Woe}} to the city of {{dam|blood}}, full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey.
The crack of the whip, the rumble of the wheel, galloping horse and bounding chariot!
Charging horseman, flashing sword, shining spear; heaps of slain, mounds of corpses, dead bodies without end, they stumble over their dead,

units.label: God exposes the harlot
units.note: I am against you, declares the LORD

verses.text: because of the many harlotries of the {{zanah|harlot}}, the seductive mistress of sorcery, who betrays nations by her prostitution and clans by her witchcraft.
“Behold, I am against you,” declares the LORD of Hosts. “I will lift your skirts over your face. I will show your nakedness to the nations and your shame to the kingdoms.
I will pelt you with filth and treat you with contempt; I will make a spectacle of you.
Then all who see you will recoil from you and say, ‘Nineveh is devastated; who will grieve for her?’ Where can I find {{nacham|comforters}} for you?”

units.label: Learn from Thebes
units.note: are you better than the city on the Nile

verses.text: Are you better than Thebes, stationed by the Nile with water around her, whose rampart was the sea, whose wall was the water?
Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength; Put and Libya were her allies.
Yet she became an exile; she went into captivity. Her infants were dashed to pieces at the head of every street. They cast lots for her dignitaries, and all her nobles were bound in chains.
You too will become drunk; you will go into hiding and seek refuge from the enemy.

units.label: Fortresses fall, locusts flee
units.note: ripe figs into the mouth, merchants like locusts

verses.text: All your fortresses are fig trees with the first ripe figs; when shaken, they fall into the mouth of the eater!
Look at your troops, they are like your women! The gates of your land are wide open to your enemies; fire consumes their bars.
Draw your water for the siege; strengthen your fortresses. Work the clay and tread the mortar; repair the brick kiln!
There the fire will devour you; the sword will cut you down and consume you like a young locust. Make yourself many like the young locust; make yourself many like the {{arbeh|swarming locust}}!
You have multiplied your merchants more than the stars of the sky. The young locust strips the land and flies away.
Your guards are like the swarming locust, and your scribes like clouds of locusts that settle on the walls on a cold day. When the sun rises, they fly away, and no one knows where.

units.label: An incurable wound
units.note: all who hear applaud your downfall

verses.text: O king of Assyria, your shepherds slumber; your officers sleep. Your people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them.
There is no healing for your injury; your wound is severe. All who hear the news of you applaud your downfall, for who has not experienced your constant cruelty?

hoy.gloss: Woe, alas, an exclamation of grief and doom often used to open a prophetic funeral lament. To pronounce hoy over a city is to announce its death in advance. Nahum opens his final oracle with this cry, framing all that follows as a dirge over Nineveh.

dam.gloss: Blood, and by extension bloodshed or guilt for murder. The Hebrew phrase is literally city of bloods, a plural pointing to countless killings. Nineveh is named for its defining sin: the shedding of innocent blood on a massive scale.

zanah.gloss: To play the harlot, to prostitute oneself. Nahum casts Nineveh as a seductive prostitute who lured and betrayed the nations, selling them enslavement dressed up as alliance. The image exposes Assyria's diplomacy and idolatry as spiritual and moral corruption.

nacham.gloss: To comfort, console, or have compassion. It is the very root of the prophet's own name, Nahum, meaning comfort. In a piercing irony, God asks where any comforters can be found for Nineveh: the city that showed no mercy will receive none, while the same word of comfort belongs to God's people.

arbeh.gloss: The swarming locust, a devouring horde that strips a land bare and then vanishes. Nahum likens Nineveh's merchants, guards, and officials to locusts: numerous, greedy, and gone in a moment when the sun rises. What seemed an unstoppable multitude simply flies away.

basic.context: This closing chapter is one long woe over Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. Nahum calls it the city of blood, full of lies and plunder, and pictures the carnage of its own conquests now turned back on itself. He reminds Nineveh of Thebes, a mighty city on the Nile that also fell, and mocks its officials as locusts that swarm and then vanish.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a prophetic funeral song for a real city that fell in 612 BC. It is not celebrating cruelty; it is declaring that the God of justice will finally repay a regime built on blood. The chilling climax is that no one will mourn Nineveh, because everyone had felt its endless cruelty.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter opens with hoy, woe, the cry of a funeral. Nineveh is the city of dam, bloods, marked by murder. She is a harlot, zanah, who seduced and betrayed the nations. And in a sharp irony God asks where comforters, from the root nacham, the very meaning of Nahum's name, can be found for her.
basic.typology: Nineveh the bloody harlot foreshadows Babylon the great in Revelation, the seductive city drunk on the blood of the saints, whose fall the whole world witnesses. Fallen Thebes and fallen Nineveh together warn every proud power that no wall or wealth can save it from God's justice.
basic.christ: The blood-guilt of Nineveh could never be healed; its wound was incurable. But the gospel is that there is healing for the guilty who turn to Christ, whose own blood was shed to cleanse the very sins that condemn. Where Nineveh found no comforter, Christ is the true comfort for all who repent, even the worst of sinners.
basic.god: We learn that God takes bloodshed and cruelty with deadly seriousness, that He exposes and shames what is proud and corrupt, and that His justice is inescapable. The mercy He longs to give, comfort, is refused only by those who refuse to repent.
basic.crossReferences: Revelation 18 shows the fall of Babylon the great, the final city of blood. Genesis 9 declares God's reckoning for shed blood. And Jesus offers rest and comfort to all who come to Him, even those with a past like Nineveh's.
basic.oneStory: The dirge over Nineveh belongs to the story of God bringing down every violent, seductive power that oppresses His people, from Nineveh to Babylon the great. Against that dark backdrop, the offer of true comfort and cleansing in Christ shines all the brighter.

context.literary:
Nahum 3 is built as a single prophetic woe that moves through five panels, and the panels are stitched together by the word of consuming. The city that was 'never without prey' in verse 1 is turned into prey by the end. Fire 'consumes' her gate bars in verse 13, fire and sword 'devour' her in verse 15, and her fortresses fall 'into the mouth of the eater' in verse 12. The predator of chapter 2, whose lion's den was filled with the kill, Nahum 2:11 to 12, is now herself on the menu.

The chapter opens at full speed. Verses 2 and 3 are almost without verbs: the crack, the rumble, the gallop, the flash, a staccato of nouns that makes the reader hear the assault. Then the pace drops into accusation and sentence in verses 4 to 7. The speaker changes at verse 5, where the LORD Himself says, 'Behold, I am against you,' the very words that closed the second chapter's oracle, Nahum 2:13. Two chapters now end their opening movements on the same divine declaration, as if God were signing each.

Verses 8 to 11 are a hinge. The pronouns shift from 'she' to 'you' at the repeated 'too' of verses 10 and 11: Thebes 'too' went into exile, and you 'too' will be drunk. The comparison does the work of a sermon illustration, and it ends by pressing the application on the hearer.

The final panels are satire. Verses 12 to 15a mock Nineveh's defences, and verses 15b to 17 turn on a taunting command, 'Make yourself many like the locust,' whose irony is that multiplying only gives the fire more to eat. Verses 18 and 19 are the dirge proper, addressed to the king, then ending in a question rather than a statement. The book of Nahum closes on a question put to Nineveh, as the book of Jonah closes on a question put to Jonah about the same city, Jonah 4:11. The two books frame the one city's story: mercy asked about, then judgment answered.
context.historical:
Nahum speaks after the fall of Thebes and before the fall of Nineveh, so he writes between about 663 and 612 BC. The Assyrian army sacked Thebes, the great religious capital of Upper Egypt, in the middle of the seventh century. It was thought untouchable, ringed by the Nile and its canals, and allied with Cush, Put and Libya, as verses 8 and 9 recall. Everyone in the ancient world knew it had fallen to Assyria, and Nahum quotes that fact back at the city that did it. The Hebrew name in verse 8 is No Amon, the city of the god Amon, which Jeremiah also knows, Jeremiah 46:25, and Ezekiel foretells a later judgment on it, Ezekiel 30:14 to 16.

Nineveh itself fell in 612 BC to a coalition of Babylonians and Medes after a siege. Assyria had ruled Judah as a heavy overlord for generations. Hezekiah's Jerusalem had been shut up by Sennacherib's army before the angel of the LORD struck it down, 2 Kings 19:35 to 37, and Manasseh had ruled as an Assyrian vassal while he 'filled Jerusalem from end to end' with innocent blood, 2 Kings 21:16. Those who first heard Nahum had grown up under the shadow of a state whose kings boasted of impaling, flaying and deporting enemies.

The images of verses 12 to 17 reflect a world of sieges and locust years. A fig tree whose first ripe fruit falls at a shake was a familiar picture of easy gain, and a locust cloud that rests on a cold morning and lifts off when the sun warms the walls was a sight any farmer knew. The line that Nineveh's troops 'are like women,' verse 13, uses a stock curse of ancient Near Eastern treaties, where the army of a covenant breaker is unmanned. Nahum borrows the curse language of the imperial treaties and turns it on the empire that imposed them.

The hearers were Judah's survivors, and the message to them was bracing: the empire you fear has an end, and the God who set that end is the God of the covenant who heard your cry.
context.canonical:
The phrase 'city of blood' is the same one Ezekiel throws at Jerusalem, 'Woe to the city of bloodshed,' Ezekiel 24:6 and 9, and Ezekiel 22:2 speaks of the city 'who brings her own doom by shedding blood within her walls.' Nahum's oracle is therefore not a special rule for foreigners. The charge that falls on Nineveh falls on Jerusalem when she copies Nineveh, and Micah says the same of the leaders who 'build Zion with bloodshed,' Micah 3:10. Habakkuk takes the very phrase up in the next book: 'Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed,' Habakkuk 2:12.

The humiliation of verse 5 recurs as a prophetic image of public shaming. God says the same of Judah, 'I will pull your skirts up over your face, that your shame may be seen,' Jeremiah 13:26, and of Babylon, 'Your nakedness will be uncovered and your shame will be exposed,' Isaiah 47:3. Ezekiel sets it in a long indictment of an unfaithful Jerusalem, Ezekiel 16:37. Nahum's metaphor is one of the standard instruments of prophetic judgment, and it falls on the powerful and the covenant people alike.

The 'I am against you' formula is shared with Jeremiah 50:31 against Babylon, Ezekiel 26:3 against Tyre, and Ezekiel 29:3 against Pharaoh. And Zephaniah 2:13 to 15, from the generation after Nahum, describes Nineveh's end in a way that matches the dirge: beasts lie down in the ruins, and everyone who passes hisses and shakes a fist.

The final question belongs with Jonah 3:10 and 4:11. The Ninevites once 'turned from their evil ways' and God relented. Nahum shows a later generation of the same city hardened into the very violence the earlier generation repented of, and the word that Jonah used for their 'evil' returns here as 'cruelty.'

In the New Testament the harlot city becomes Babylon in Revelation 17 and 18, who is 'drunk with the blood of the saints,' Revelation 17:6, and whose fall draws the cry 'Hallelujah!' Revelation 19:1 to 2, the heavenly version of the applause in Nahum 3:19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Nahum wrote to people who had lived under Assyria's boot and were tempted to conclude that power decides everything. His chief aim was to tell them that Nineveh's wealth, her fortresses, her allies and her bureaucrats were all provisional. The comparison with Thebes is his proof. A city that seemed more secure than Nineveh, with water for a wall and half of Africa for allies, was taken by the very empire he is now addressing. If it happened to Thebes, he says, why should it not happen to you?

He also meant to correct a quiet cynicism among his own people. If the strong are never held to account, then trust in the LORD is a luxury. Nahum answers that the God who takes the side of the oppressed is neither blind nor late, and he does it by making the empire's own methods the shape of its ruin: the city that dashed infants at street corners will see her sons fall, the city that shamed nations will be shamed, and the city that devoured will be devoured.

Nahum is not neutral about the people he addresses. He speaks to Judah with the earlier promise of Nahum 1:15 still ringing, that the wicked will never again march through her. The oracle against Nineveh is good news in the ears of the afflicted. It is not written to push Nineveh toward repentance, as Jonah's was; it is written so that the hurting hear that evil has an expiry date.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what God will do to one empire. It does not command Israel to take up arms against the nations, and nothing in it licenses a believer to gloat over an enemy's pain. The applause of verse 19 is a prediction of what all the victims will do, not an order to clap, and the Bible elsewhere warns against rejoicing when an enemy falls, Proverbs 24:17.

What the passage does teach is the pattern by which God judges. He judges cruelty by cruelty returned, pride by public exposure, and trust in strength by the collapse of that strength. These are statements about how history bends, and they invite two responses. Those who suffer under injustice are told to hold on, since the oppressor will not last. Those who hold power are told that the measure they use will be used on them.

It is also worth noticing what is not prescribed. Nahum gives Judah no military plan. The deliverance comes from God, through other nations, at a time He chooses. The right response is the one Nahum 1:7 sets down: the LORD is good, 'a stronghold in the day of distress,' and He cares for those who trust in Him.

debates.question: Does Nahum 3 show a God who delights in destruction?

views.label: It shows a God who is just toward real victims
views.case: Every charge in the chapter is specific: blood, lies, plunder, betrayal of nations, infants dashed in the street. God's wrath is the answer to those wrongs, and the closing line asks 'who has not experienced your constant cruelty?' On this view the joy at the end is moral relief, the gladness of Proverbs 11:10, 'when the wicked perish, there are shouts of joy.' A God who never judged such things would be unjust, and Revelation 19:1 to 2 puts the same joy in heaven: 'His judgments are true and just.'

views.label: It is dark rhetoric that must be read against Jonah
views.case: Others hear the book as the voice of an aggrieved people, one that sits uneasily beside the God who 'cares' about Nineveh, Jonah 4:11. They note that the same God spared Nineveh after Jonah, and that Nahum never mentions the earlier repentance. Read together, the books show the two sides of one character, slow to anger yet not leaving the guilty unpunished, Nahum 1:3.

debates.bearing: The two views are closer than they look. Nahum 1:3 holds patience and justice in the same breath, and chapter 3 describes what happens when patience is answered by a later generation of the same cruelty. The chapter should be read as justice for the oppressed, with Jonah as the standing proof that the door of mercy had been open.

debates.question: Is the 'harlot' a literal charge of sexual sin or a political image?

views.label: A political and religious metaphor
views.case: Verse 4 says she 'betrays nations by her prostitution and clans by her witchcraft.' Prophets regularly use harlotry for treaties, trade and idol worship that exploit others, Isaiah 23:17 of Tyre for example. Assyria's diplomacy, bought by flattery and enforced by violence, and her devotion to divination and the gods of conquest fit the image without any sexual reading.

views.label: A literal and a cultural charge
views.case: Some interpreters add that Nineveh's religion included temple prostitution and that the harlot image is rooted in fact as well as symbol. The text itself speaks only of 'harlotries' and 'witchcraft,' and the link with sorcery is already found in 2 Kings 9:22, where the harlotries and sorceries of Jezebel are named together.

debates.bearing: The text's grammar points to metaphor, since what she 'sells' are nations and clans. What matters for application is that the image treats seduction and violence as one sin: a power that wins by charm and keeps by force.

study.originalLanguages:
Nahum 3:1 calls Nineveh full of lies and plunder, and the Hebrew is more pointed than the English. The word for lies is kachash, the deceit of denial and flattery, the diplomat's mask. The plunder is pereq, a tearing apart, the word used elsewhere for a crossroads where fugitives are cut off, Obadiah 1:14. Deceit and tearing are the two arms of the empire, charm to win and violence to keep. The city is 'never without prey,' teref, the lion's word, and Nahum had already used it of the lion's den, Nahum 2:12 and 13. Here the city that stores its prey loses it.

In verse 4 the harlot 'betrays' nations, but the participle is mokheret, 'selling.' She sold nations through her harlotry and clans through her witchcraft, kesheph, a word already joined to harlotry in 2 Kings 9:22 for Jezebel. The treaty partner who was courted was in fact being traded. In verse 5 the shaming image, 'I will lift your skirts over your face,' also appears in Jeremiah 13:26 and Isaiah 47:2 to 3, and the fact that all three prophets use it shows how formal an image of judgment it had become.

Verse 6 says God will pelt her with 'filth,' shiqqutsim. The word elsewhere names detestable things, above all idols, as in Deuteronomy 29:17. The BSB gives the sense, but the Hebrew hints that the objects of her devotion become the thing thrown at her.

Verse 7 asks 'who will grieve for her?' with a verb, nud, that means to shake the head in sympathy or to bemoan. In Job 2:11 it appears beside the word for comfort when his friends come to 'sympathize with him and comfort him.' So the question has two parts: no one will bemoan her, and no one will be found to comfort her. The prophet's name and the verb for comfort already meet in that sentence, which the basic text points out.

The hinge of verses 10 and 11 is the Hebrew gam, 'also,' repeated: 'she too' went into exile, 'you too' will be drunk. Gam turns a historical report into a sentence, the rhetoric of 'what happened to her will happen to you.' The word for fortresses falling 'like fig trees' in verse 12 uses bikkurim, the firstfruits, ripe before the harvest and fallen at a touch. In verse 17 the 'swarming locust,' gobai, and the 'young locust,' yeleq of verse 15, are two of the several locust words that Joel 1:4 lists in sequence, so Nahum is sounding the cry of a locust year in many voices.

Verse 19 ends the book with a Hebrew sentence in which the last word is the one for 'continually.' The Hebrew speaks of her 'evil' passing over everyone without stop, the noun ra'ah, the same family of words used of Nineveh's 'wickedness' in Jonah 1:2 and of the 'evil ways' they turned from in Jonah 3:10. The BSB's 'cruelty' is a fair rendering, but the root is the one that connects Nahum to the story of Jonah. And the injury is a shever, a fracture, the same word used of an incurable break in Jeremiah 30:12 to 13.

typology.fulfillment: Nineveh is the seductive, bloodstained power in a prophet's vision, and Revelation draws the same figure larger. The 'great prostitute' of Revelation 17:1 to 6 sits on many waters, makes kings drunk with the wine of her immorality, and is 'drunk with the blood of the saints.' The correspondence is that a world power wins by attraction and keeps by killing. The escalation is that John's Babylon gathers every empire's trade and cruelty, Revelation 18:24, until it stands for the whole order opposed to God. The type falls short because Nineveh was one city with a date of death, while Babylon in Revelation is a pattern that outlasts any one capital.

typology.type: Fallen Thebes as a warning, Nahum 3:8 to 10
typology.fulfillment: The fall of a mighty city is set before Nineveh as a mirror. Thebes thought itself safe behind water and allies, and Nineveh was the sword that proved otherwise. In the Bible this mirror recurs. Babylon, the next to be conquered, is told her turn comes, Isaiah 13:19, and in Revelation the one who says 'I sit as queen' is warned, Revelation 18:7 to 8. Escalation comes in Revelation 16:19, where 'the cities of the nations collapsed' in one stroke. The correspondence breaks down only in that Thebes and Nineveh were judged by earthly armies, while the final judgment comes directly from the throne.

Other prophets use the same phrase for Judah, Egypt and Samaria, Jeremiah 30:12, 46:11 and Micah 1:9, so the incurable break is a standing picture of sin that no human remedy can mend. In Christ the picture reverses. The One who 'was pierced for our transgressions' bore a wound that heals, 'by His stripes we are healed,' Isaiah 53:5, and Peter applies it to the cross, 1 Peter 2:24. The type falls short in one respect: Nineveh's wound was the result of her own deeds with no remedy offered in Nahum, while Christ takes the wound for others.

typology.type: The locust crowd that flies away, Nahum 3:15 to 17
typology.fulfillment: The great mass of officials and merchants proves to be a swarm that rests only until the sun is warm, then vanishes. Jesus teaches the same lesson about earthly security in the parable of the rich fool, who stored up for himself and lost his soul that night, Luke 12:16 to 21. The correspondence is that numbers and wealth are no protection against the day of God. The escalation is that the loss is no longer a city's but a person's, and the answer is not a stronger wall but being 'rich toward God,' Luke 12:21.

study.christ:
Nahum 3 leads to Christ by contrast first. Nineveh's last line is that there is no healing and no comforter. The prophet's own name means 'comfort,' and yet at the centre of his closing oracle that comfort has been withdrawn, verse 7. The gospel reverses it. Isaiah's 'Comfort, comfort My people,' Isaiah 40:1, is fulfilled in the One whom Simeon waited for as 'the consolation of Israel,' Luke 2:25. Jesus says, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28, and Paul calls the Father 'the God of all comfort,' 2 Corinthians 1:3. A city that lived by bloodshed found no one to grieve for her. Jesus, standing over a different city, 'wept over it,' Luke 19:41, and spoke as one who would gladly have gathered it, Matthew 23:37. The mourning that Nineveh could not find is given to Jerusalem by the Lord Himself.

It leads to Christ by the theme of the bleeding wound. Nahum's 'there is no healing for your injury' is the language of an incurable fracture, shever. The cross is God's answer to precisely that: Christ 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' and 'by His stripes you are healed,' 1 Peter 2:24, drawing on Isaiah 53:5. The prophet's wound could not be bound. The wound in Christ's side and hands was borne so that others' could be.

It leads to Christ by the shape of justice. The cruelty of Nineveh is answered in kind, but the cross shows a justice that does not simply return the blow. In Romans 3:26 God acts 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus.' The justice Nahum announces is real, and the cross is where it is both carried out and where mercy is opened to the guilty. This is why Jonah's story can stand beside Nahum's. The door of repentance was open for Nineveh, Jonah 3:10, and the door is open still.

And it leads to Christ by the final victory. The heavenly shout of Revelation 19:1 to 2 comes when 'He has avenged the blood of His servants.' The Lamb who was slain is the one who judges, so the cries of the martyrs, 'How long, O Lord,' Revelation 6:10, are answered by the same Christ whose own blood was shed by a violent empire, Acts 4:27 to 28.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Nineveh is not a type of Christ, and the harlot is not an allegory of any one modern power. The links above lie in the New Testament's own use of the themes: comfort, healing, justice, and the avenging of innocent blood.
study.god:
Nahum 3 shows a God who is the defender of the people no one else would defend. The fury of the chapter is aimed at specific crimes, bloodshed, deceit and trade in human lives, and it is the other side of His love. A God who did not rise against cruelty would not be good, and the book that opens with 'The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress,' Nahum 1:7, closes with His arrival against the oppressor. The two are one portrait.

He is the God who speaks in the first person against evil. 'Behold, I am against you' is a covenant formula, since only the God of Israel can set His face against an empire and mean it. In it He is also free: Assyria had been His 'rod of anger' for a time, Isaiah 10:5, and yet He holds the rod to account for the arrogance with which it was swung, Isaiah 10:12 to 15. The tool never becomes the owner, and God never becomes the accomplice of the one He uses.

He is the God of history. The fall of Thebes and the coming fall of Nineveh are not coincidences of strategy but a design: 'this is the plan devised for the whole earth,' Isaiah 14:26. The empire that boasted that it moved nations is itself moved. Yet the means are ordinary ones, a siege, a fire, a coalition. God's rule over nations is not a rival to history but its hidden hand.

He is the God who gives people what they chose. The measures of the chapter fit the crime, which is what moral order looks like when it is God's: the city that made a spectacle of others is made a spectacle, and the strength that rested on figs and locusts is exposed as figs and locusts. This is no petty retaliation. It shows that the world is built so that violence cannot finally win.

And He is patient. Nahum 1:3 says 'slow to anger,' and Jonah 4:11 gives the evidence: He cared for the city enough to send a prophet. The wound of Nahum 3:19 is not where God began with Nineveh. It is where a generation that had once repented and then went back to violence ended.

For worship, the chapter teaches those who are hurt to pray as the martyrs do, 'How long, O Lord,' Revelation 6:10, and to expect an answer. It teaches the powerful to fear Him. And it teaches everyone to take refuge in the One who 'cares for those who trust in Him,' Nahum 1:7, rather than in fortresses or numbers.

crossReferences.note: The lion's den filled with the kill and the line 'I am against you' that Nahum repeats in 3:5. The earlier chapter shows the predator and the sentence; chapter 3 shows the same sentence carried out as a siege. Both end the same way, with 'prey' cut off from the earth.

'Woe to the city of bloodshed' is Ezekiel's cry over Jerusalem, in the very phrase Nahum applies to Nineveh. It shows the standard does not change with the nation: bloodshed in a city that belongs to God is judged as bloodshed in the city that does not.

The shaming of Babylon, with the veil removed and shame exposed, uses the same image as Nahum 3:5. The coupling of the two prophets shows how the passing of one empire, Assyria, sets the pattern for the next, Babylon.

Names Amon, god of Thebes, among those God will punish, tying the Thebes of Nahum 3:8 to the larger story of Egypt's gods under judgment. Nahum's rhetorical question about Thebes rests on a city whose fall was widely remembered.

A parallel dirge over Nineveh from the generation after Nahum: she is a 'carefree city' that says 'I am it, and there is none besides me,' and she becomes a place for beasts. It shows the confident pride that Nahum's questions are aimed at, and its result.

The book of Jonah ends with a question about Nineveh, and Nahum with a question about her cruelty. Read together they show a city given a chance, 'more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left,' and the later generation that threw it away.

Explains how God can use Assyria and then judge her. Assyria boasted, 'By the strength of my hand I have done this,' and God asks whether an axe can boast over the one who swings it. This is the theology behind Nahum 3's sentence on the empire's pride.

John's great prostitute, drunk with the blood of the saints, is Nahum's harlot city on a world scale. She sits on many waters and holds a golden cup full of abominations. The Old Testament city becomes the pattern for the last opposition to Christ.

The multitude in heaven shouts 'Hallelujah' because God has avenged the blood of His servants. This is the heavenly equivalent of the applause in Nahum 3:19, and it shows that the joy at the fall of a violent power is joy in God's justice.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, the opposite of Nineveh's 'who will grieve for her?' He grieves because the city did not recognise the time of its visitation. Where Nahum announces that no one mourns a ruined oppressor, Jesus mourns even for a city that will reject Him.

'By His stripes you are healed' answers 'There is no healing for your injury.' The incurable wound of sin is borne by Christ on the tree. Peter echoes Isaiah 53:5 and shows where the healing that Nineveh lacked can be found.

study.oneStory:
Nahum 3 stands inside the story of the nations that began at Babel. In Genesis 11 humanity gathers to build a city and a tower and make a name, and God scatters them. From then on the Bible traces the line of cities that try to do the same: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Tyre, and at the end the Babylon of Revelation. Nineveh was built by Nimrod, according to Genesis 10:11, and from the very start of the story it was a city of the world's power. Nahum's chapter is the point at which the story delivers its verdict on one of them.

The chapter answers a question the Bible keeps raising: what becomes of those who shed innocent blood? God told Noah, 'Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed,' Genesis 9:6, and blood cries out from the ground as early as Cain, Genesis 4:10. Nahum shows that the cry is heard even when it rises from conquered peoples far from home. It also answers the fear of Judah that Assyria had won for good, since Isaiah 10 had already said that the rod would be broken, Isaiah 10:24 to 27.

It sets up what follows. Babylon rises on Nineveh's ruins and becomes the next tool and the next target, as Habakkuk goes on to show: the woe over the city built with blood, Habakkuk 2:12, is Nahum's woe transferred. Then the thread runs through Daniel, where the statue of the nations is broken, and into Revelation, where 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,' Revelation 18:2. The sequence teaches that no empire is the last one, and that the same God ends them all.

At the same time the chapter points past judgment to healing. The one wound that cannot be healed in Nahum is the wound that Christ bears in Isaiah 53:5. Nineveh finds no comfort; the church is told, 'Come out of her, My people,' Revelation 18:4, and is promised the God who 'will wipe away every tear,' Revelation 21:4.

The new creation completes the story in two ways. The harlot city is replaced by the holy city, the bride, 'prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2, and the nations that once came as plunder bring their glory in freely, Revelation 21:24 and 26. The blood that cried out is answered, and the mourning that no one gave is given by God Himself.

quiz.q: Why is Nineveh called the city of blood in verse 1?

options.text: The Hebrew reads city of bloods, marking Assyria's massive, defining guilt of shed innocent blood.
options.note: The plural points to murder heaped on murder, the empire's characteristic sin.

options.text: Because much blood was shed in her many wars and conquests.
options.note: On the right track: it refers to bloodshed, specifically Nineveh's guilt for shed innocent blood.

options.text: Because it was built beside a red river.
options.note: The reference is to violence and killing, not geography.

options.text: It is an empty insult with no basis.
options.note: Assyria's documented atrocities fully ground the charge.

quiz.q: Why does Nahum point Nineveh to the fall of Thebes in verses 8-10?

options.text: As a warning: a mighty, well-defended city already fell, so Nineveh is not safe either.
options.note: Thebes, with the Nile as her wall, still fell; so will Nineveh.

options.text: To praise Thebes as greater than Nineveh.
options.note: The point is not praise but warning by parallel.

options.text: To recall a great city Assyria itself conquered, now a warning of Nineveh's own turn.
options.note: True that Assyria took Thebes; the point is the warning that Nineveh will fall in the same way.

options.text: It is an unrelated historical aside.
options.note: It is a deliberate warning that no fortress guarantees survival.

quiz.q: What is the striking irony in God's question, where can I find comforters for you, in verse 7?

options.text: It uses the root of Nahum's name, comfort; the city that gave no mercy will receive none.
options.note: The prophet of comfort announces that no comfort remains for the impenitent city.

options.text: It means God is desperately searching for someone to help Nineveh.
options.note: It is a rhetorical question declaring that no comforter will be found.

options.text: It is a rhetorical question whose answer is that none are left to comfort her.
options.note: Right that none will comfort her, but it also plays on Nahum's name, comfort.

options.text: It has nothing to do with the prophet's name.
options.note: Nahum means comfort, and the wordplay is deliberate.

quiz.q: What do the locust images in verses 15-17 say about Nineveh's officials and merchants?

options.text: They are a greedy, numberless horde that strips the land and then vanishes at sunrise.
options.note: The locust pictures multitude and plunder followed by sudden disappearance.

options.text: They are hard-working farmers feeding the city.
options.note: The locust devours and flees; it is a picture of plunder, not provision.

options.text: They are a vast multitude, but one that plunders and then abandons the city.
options.note: Right that they are a great multitude; the sting is that they strip the land and flee.

options.text: They guarantee the city's permanence.
options.note: The locusts flee and no one knows where; nothing is guaranteed.

quiz.q: How does Nineveh's incurable wound point us to Christ?

options.text: Its blood-guilt could not be healed, but Christ's wounds heal even the guiltiest who repent, Isaiah 53:5.
options.note: The difference is repentance and faith, not the size of the sin.

options.text: It warns that unrepented sin stays incurable, though Christ heals all who turn to Him.
options.note: Close: impenitence leaves the wound incurable, but the sin's size is no barrier to Christ.

options.text: It shows God never really heals anyone.
options.note: The gospel offers real healing to all who turn to Christ.

options.text: It has no connection to the gospel.
options.note: The contrast with Christ's healing wounds is the very point.

questions: Nahum names Nineveh's defining sin plainly: blood, lies, and plunder. What sin, if named honestly, would define the pattern of your own life, and what would it mean to bring it to God?
Thebes seemed unconquerable, yet it fell. What are you leaning on as though it could never fail, and how does Nineveh's warning reorder your trust?
God asks where comforters can be found for Nineveh, and the answer is nowhere, because she would not repent. How does the door of repentance still standing open for you move your heart today?
The world applauded when the cruel empire fell. How do you hold together honest longing for justice with the warning not to gloat over any person's downfall?
Nineveh's wound was incurable, yet by Christ's wounds even the worst sinner can be healed. Is there a guilt you have thought beyond forgiveness, that the blood of Jesus is able to cleanse?

translationNotes.note: City of blood renders the Hebrew city of bloods, the plural indicating repeated, massive bloodshed rather than a single act.
Thebes is the Hebrew No-amon, the great Egyptian city on the Nile that fell to Assyria in 663 BC, cited as a fresh and undeniable example of a mighty city brought down.
Guards and scribes render Hebrew terms that may also mean princes and marshals; the point is that Nineveh's officials, however titled, scatter like locusts at sunrise.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Nahum 3:1-19. Poetic line fragments joined into running verse text.
